Apollo 8 Mission Report (MSC-PA-R-69-1), Table 3-1 sequence of events, NTRS 19700033031
Kennedy Space Center, 1968-12-21 12:51:00 UTC (7:51 a.m. EST). Saturn V AS-503 lifts Borman, Lovell and Anders into a 98 x 103 nmi Earth parking orbit 11 min 35 s later,.
S-IVB reignites at GET 2:50:37 (1968-12-21 15:41 UTC) for a 319-second burn that sends the first crew toward the Moon.
SPS burn at GET 10:59:59 (1968-12-21 23:50 UTC), 24.8 ft/s (7.6 m/s), lowering the planned pericynthion from 459 to 66.3 nmi.
RCS trim at GET 60:59:56 (1968-12-24 01:50 UTC), 1.4 ft/s (0.4 m/s), refining the lunar orbit insertion conditions.
1968-12-24 09:59 UTC, GET 69:08:20. A 246.9-second SPS burn behind the Moon captures Apollo 8 into a 168.5 x 60.0 nmi lunar orbit; a circularization at GET 73:35:07 follows to 59.7 x 60.7 nmi.
1968-12-25 06:10 UTC, GET 89:19:17. A 204-second SPS burn on the far side ends 20 h 11 min and ten revolutions in lunar orbit and sends the crew home.
The only trans-earth correction (the report calls it the third), 4.8 ft/s (1.5 m/s) at GET 103:59:54, 1968-12-25 20:50 UTC.
1968-12-27 15:51 UTC, GET 147:00:42. The command module enters at 146:46:13 and lands under parachutes, closing the 6.1-day first crewed flight to the Moon.
First humans to leave low Earth orbit + orbit the Moon

Apollo 8 was a bet placed in a hurry. Intelligence suggested the Soviets might loop a crew around the Moon first, so in the summer of 1968 NASA tore up the flight plan and sent three men to lunar orbit on only the third launch of a rocket that had never carried a crew. It should have been reckless. Instead it became the year's one piece of good news — 1968 had been assassinations, Vietnam, cities on fire — and on Christmas Eve an estimated billion people heard Genesis read from lunar orbit and, in Bill Anders' photograph, watched their whole world rise over a dead horizon for the first time. Apollo 11 is remembered for the Moon. Apollo 8 is the one that showed us the Earth.

The first crewed mission to leave low Earth orbit, the first to escape Earth gravity, and the first to orbit the Moon. Launched 1968-12-21 on the first crewed flight of the Saturn V (AS-503), Apollo 8 entered lunar orbit on Christmas Eve 1968. Anders' "Earthrise" photograph during the fourth orbit became one of the most influential images in history. The crew read from Genesis on live television to an estimated audience of up to a billion — the most-watched broadcast to that date. 10 orbits later they fired the SPS engine for TEI on the far side of the Moon, returning to Pacific splashdown 1968-12-27. NASA had decided in August 1968 to swap Apollo 8's payload from a high-Earth-orbit LM test to a lunar-orbit CSM-only mission after CIA intelligence suggested the USSR might attempt a circumlunar flight first.
Saturn V (AS-503) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39A 1968-12-21 12:51 UTC — first crewed Saturn V flight.
Trans-lunar injection burn — first crewed escape of Earth gravity. S-IVB ∆v ~3.05 km/s.
Lunar orbit insertion behind the Moon, out of radio contact. SPS burn ~0.91 km/s. First humans to orbit another body.
Anders photographs Earth rising over the lunar horizon during the fourth orbit (1968-12-24, AS08-14-2383).
Crew reads from Genesis on live TV to an estimated audience of up to a billion — the most-watched broadcast to that date.
Trans-Earth injection behind the Moon (1968-12-25 06:10 UTC). SPS ∆v ~1.07 km/s.
CM splashed down in North Pacific 1968-12-27. Recovery by USS Yorktown.
